title: Weighted Event Scoring
summary:
Weighted event scoring turns **many events of unequal value** into one score per item or user: a purchase is worth far more than a view. The basic form is

`score = sum over events ( weight(type) x decay(age) )`

with example weights view = 1, click = 3, add-to-cart = 5, purchase = 10. Raw counts rank by volume; weighted scores rank by value.

**Time decay.** Recent events matter more. With a half-life `H`, an event aged `t` is multiplied by `0.5^(t/H)`. Exponential decay has a handy property: you can keep just `(score, last_update)` and update lazily, `score = score x 0.5^(dt/H) + weight`, the same trick as a lazily refilled [token bucket](#/sd/f/rate-limiter), instead of re-reading every event.

**Guardrails.**
- **Cap or dampen** repeated events (`min(count, cap)` or `log(1+count)`) so one user clicking 1,000 times cannot dominate.
- **Deduplicate** by event id because delivery is at least once.
- Choose weights from outcomes (how strongly each event predicts conversion) and revisit them; they are product decisions, not constants of nature.
- Scores are only comparable if events are measured on the same scale and window.

The result feeds [top-k ranking](#/sd/f/top-k-ranking); recent windows can be maintained with [sliding-window aggregation](#/sd/f/sliding-window-aggregation).

drills.q: Weights: view = 1, click = 3, purchase = 10. Item A has 100 views, 10 clicks and 1 purchase. Item B has 20 views, 5 clicks and 12 purchases. Which statement is right?
options: A ranks first on both raw event count and weighted score
They tie, since the weights cancel out
A ranks first by weighted score (140 vs 65)
B ranks first by weighted score (155 vs 140), although A has far more raw events
drills.explain: A = 100 + 30 + 10 = 140. B = 20 + 15 + 120 = 155. Raw counts are 111 versus 37, so volume would rank A first; weighting by value flips the order.

drills.q: An event with weight 10 happened 21 days ago. The score uses exponential decay with a half-life of 7 days, `weight x 0.5^(age/half-life)`. What is its current contribution?

Lazy decayed score: an item's score was 8 at time 0. The half-life is 1 hour. At t = 2 hours a new event of weight 5 arrives; the update is `score = score x 0.5^(dt/H) + weight`. What is the new score?
drills.explain: Two half-lives pass: 8 x 0.25 = 2, plus 5 = 7. This needs only the previous (score, timestamp), not the event history.

drills.q: One bot account clicks the same product 5,000 times in a minute and the product shoots to the top of the trending list. Which change fixes this class of problem most directly?
options: Cap or dampen per-user, per-item event counts (e.g. log(1+n)) and deduplicate by event id
drills.explain: The weighting is fine; the input is unbounded. Per-user caps and dedup limit the influence of any single actor. A shorter half-life only makes the spike fade sooner.

drills.q: Put the stages of a trending-items pipeline in order.
items: Ingest events and deduplicate by event id
Multiply each event by its type weight
Apply time decay and add to the item's running score
Select the top k items by score
drills.explain: Dedup and capping must come before weighting so a duplicate or spammy event never contributes. Ranking is the last step.

drills.q: Why use weights instead of raw event counts, and what does exponential decay add?
drills.answer: Events differ in value (a purchase signals far more intent than a view), so weights make the score reflect value, not volume. Decay with a half-life makes recent activity count more and, being exponential, can be updated incrementally from `(score, last_update)` without scanning event history. Guardrails: cap per-user repeats, deduplicate, and re-tune the weights against real outcomes.
